source_refs.note: Book p. 192: 10.5 Half Angle Identities, lead-in sentence and (i) cos a/2, (ii) sin a/2, (iii) tan a/2 with +/- roots; 10.6 begins below on the same page

blocks.text: The formulas proved above can also be written in the form of half angle identities, in the following way:

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: In the double angle formulas, \(\alpha\) is half of \(2\alpha\). Writing \(\alpha\) in place of \(2\alpha\) (and so \(\frac{\alpha}{2}\) in place of \(\alpha\)) gives \(\cos\alpha = 2\cos^{2}\frac{\alpha}{2} - 1 = 1 - 2\sin^{2}\frac{\alpha}{2}\). Solving these for \(\cos\frac{\alpha}{2}\) and \(\sin\frac{\alpha}{2}\) gives the half angle identities: they find the ratios of half an angle from the cosine of the whole angle.

blocks.text_alt: cos of alpha over 2 equals plus or minus the square root of (1 plus cos alpha) over 2
sin of alpha over 2 equals plus or minus the square root of (1 minus cos alpha) over 2
tan of alpha over 2 equals plus or minus the square root of (1 minus cos alpha) over (1 plus cos alpha)

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Choosing the sign: the sign in front of the root is not decided by the formula. It is decided by the quadrant in which \(\frac{\alpha}{2}\) lies (not \(\alpha\)).
Example: for \(\alpha = 240^{\circ}\), \(\cos\alpha = -\frac{1}{2}\) and \(\frac{\alpha}{2} = 120^{\circ}\) is in quadrant II, where cosine is negative:
\[\cos 120^{\circ} = -\sqrt{\dfrac{1 - \frac{1}{2}}{2}} = -\dfrac{1}{2}\]
Taking \(+\) here would give a wrong answer.

blocks.title: Exam tip
blocks.text:
Half angle identities give the exact ratios of \(15^{\circ}\) from \(\cos 30^{\circ} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\):
\[\cos 15^{\circ} = \sqrt{\dfrac{1 + \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}}{2}} = \dfrac{\sqrt{2 + \sqrt{3}}}{2}\]
\[\sin 15^{\circ} = \sqrt{\dfrac{1 - \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}}{2}} = \dfrac{\sqrt{2 - \sqrt{3}}}{2}\]
\[\tan 15^{\circ} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2 - \sqrt{3}}{2 + \sqrt{3}}} = 2 - \sqrt{3}\]
(all signs \(+\) because \(15^{\circ}\) is in quadrant I). These agree with \(\cos 15^{\circ} = \frac{\sqrt{6}+\sqrt{2}}{4}\) and \(\sin 15^{\circ} = \frac{\sqrt{6}-\sqrt{2}}{4}\) obtained from \(45^{\circ} - 30^{\circ}\).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Two forms of \(\tan\frac{\alpha}{2}\) without a square root (not in the book, but useful): multiplying top and bottom of \(\frac{\sin(\alpha/2)}{\cos(\alpha/2)}\) by \(2\cos\frac{\alpha}{2}\) or by \(2\sin\frac{\alpha}{2}\) gives
\[\tan\dfrac{\alpha}{2} = \dfrac{\sin\alpha}{1 + \cos\alpha} = \dfrac{1 - \cos\alpha}{\sin\alpha}\]
These carry the correct sign automatically.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. Half angle identities are the forms \(2\cos^{2}\alpha - 1\) and \(1 - 2\sin^{2}\alpha\) of \(\cos 2\alpha\), written for the angle \(\frac{\alpha}{2}\).
2. \(\cos\frac{\alpha}{2} = \pm\sqrt{\frac{1 + \cos\alpha}{2}}\), \(\sin\frac{\alpha}{2} = \pm\sqrt{\frac{1 - \cos\alpha}{2}}\), \(\tan\frac{\alpha}{2} = \pm\sqrt{\frac{1 - \cos\alpha}{1 + \cos\alpha}}\).
3. Plus inside goes with cosine, minus inside goes with sine.
4. The sign is chosen from the quadrant of \(\frac{\alpha}{2}\).

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Choosing the sign from the quadrant of \(\alpha\) instead of \(\frac{\alpha}{2}\).
2. Forgetting the 2 in the denominator of \(\frac{1 \pm \cos\alpha}{2}\) (it is not there in the \(\tan\) formula).
3. Interchanging \(1 + \cos\alpha\) and \(1 - \cos\alpha\) between the sine and cosine formulas. Test with \(\alpha = 0\): \(\cos 0 = 1\) needs \(\sqrt{\frac{1+1}{2}} = 1\).
